RPMac - Quick start
===================

1. Keep RPMac.exe, smccore.exe and inpout32.dll TOGETHER in the same folder.
2. Right-click RPMac.exe  ->  "Run as administrator"
   (administrator rights are required to access the Mac's hardware/SMC).
3. Set each fan to Auto / Max / a custom RPM, or use "Curve" to ramp the fan
   with temperature:
     - drag a point to move it
     - double-click the graph to add a point
     - right-click a point to remove it
   The red dot shows where the fan is running on the curve right now. Pick a
   sensor, or leave "Highest temp" so the fan follows whichever component is
   hottest.
   Tip: save your setup as a named preset and switch profiles with one click
   (also from the tray icon: right-click -> Presets).

The sidebar has four pages: Fans, Sensors, Presets and Settings.

Worth turning on in Settings
----------------------------
- "Smooth fan changes" (on by default) stops the fan hunting up and down when
  the temperature wobbles by a degree.
- "Emergency cooling" sends every fan to maximum if any sensor reaches the
  temperature you pick, whatever mode the fans are in.
- "Record to a CSV file" appends every reading to history.csv, so you can look
  back at what ran hot during a game or a long render.

Scripting (optional)
--------------------
smccore.exe is a command-line tool for the same control, e.g.:
   smccore.exe list                 show fans
   smccore.exe set 0 2000           fan 0 -> 2000 RPM
   smccore.exe auto 0               fan 0 -> automatic
   smccore.exe max                  all fans -> maximum
Run it from an administrator terminal, with inpout32.dll in the folder.

Requirements
------------
- An Intel Mac running Windows (Boot Camp).
- On non-Apple PCs the app stays READ-ONLY and changes nothing.

If Windows blocks it
--------------------
RPMac is a small open-source app and is not code-signed (a certificate costs
a few hundred dollars a year), so Windows does not recognise it yet.

- SmartScreen ("Windows protected your PC")
    -> click "More info", then "Run anyway".
- Smart App Control ("An Application Control policy has blocked this file")
    -> the app silently refuses to start. Either turn Smart App Control off in
       Windows Security > App & browser control, or build RPMac yourself from
       the source (instructions in the repository README).
- Antivirus: RPMac uses InpOut32, a low-level I/O driver, to talk to the Mac's
  SMC (the chip that controls the fans). Some antivirus tools flag this kind of
  driver as "potentially unwanted" because it grants hardware access. This is
  normal for fan-control utilities; allow it manually if it gets blocked.

None of this means something is wrong with the app - it is what happens to any
unsigned utility that talks to hardware. Everything RPMac does is public:
https://github.com/golirt1/RPMAC

Safety
------
Running the fan at maximum is safe for the hardware, but constant max speed
means more noise and wear over time. RPMac never disables the SMC's built-in
thermal protection.
